Lord Byron, of 'Childe Harold's Pilgrimage' Romantic poetry
context: Lord Dunsany (1878-1957) was the godfather of secondary-world fantasy. His 1924 novel The King of Elfland's Daughter is the canonical depiction of Faerie as an alien-beautiful realm with skies of unearthly light. Gygax cited Dunsany in the original DMG Appendix N. The Vault of the Drow itself, as a place, became an iconic image: the dark elves' city, beautiful and corrupt, lit by an artificial gem-and-fungus 'sky.' Players who have visited the Vault in the original D3 often remember the scene better than any combat encounter.

question: From 1986 until 2003, Dragon Magazine ran an iconic rules-and-canon Q&A column called 'Sage Advice,' answering reader questions about AD&D rules clarifications, monster stats, and setting canon. The column was written almost continuously by a single TSR/WotC designer who became the unofficial 'rules guru' of D&D for an entire generation of players. Who wrote Sage Advice for those 17 years?
answer: Skip Williams, who later co-designed 3rd Edition D&D
choices: Skip Williams, who later co-designed 3rd Edition D&D
Roger E. Moore, who edited Dragon Magazine through the same era
Kim Mohan, who edited Dragon Magazine in the 1980s
Bruce Heard, of the Voyage of the Princess Ark Mystara column
context: Skip Williams joined TSR in the early 1980s and became the company's rules-arbitration specialist. He co-authored the 2000 D&D 3rd Edition Monster Manual with Jonathan Tweet and Monte Cook. Williams' Sage Advice column was infamous for both authoritative rulings and occasional reversals — letters would prompt re-rulings months later. The column resumed in 5e under Jeremy Crawford, but the classic-era Sage Advice with Williams remains the iconic version.

question: TSR's 1989 Spelljammer setting cosmology had Dungeons & Dragons solar systems enclosed in vast immobile 'crystal spheres' floating in an interstitial medium called the phlogiston. Ships traveled the phlogiston using a magical helm — a chair-shaped item that converted the pilot's spell energy into ship motion. Helms ranged from cheap minor helms to powerful major helms. Who built the high-end major helms in canonical Spelljammer lore?
answer: The Arcane — gigantic blue-skinned alien merchants who sell helms throughout the spheres
choices: The Arcane — gigantic blue-skinned alien merchants who sell helms throughout the spheres
The Mercane — the canonical Spelljammer name for a different blue-skinned race
The Neogi — spider-slavers who manufacture helms via dark magic
The Giff — Napoleonic hippopotamus-mercenaries who fabricate helms
context: The Arcane are 15-foot tall blue-skinned humanoids with too-long limbs. They speak with their own dialect of the Auld trade tongue and value gold above all other commodities. They monopolize the helm market across all of crystal-sphere space. The 2022 5e Spelljammer reboot renamed them 'Mercane' (canonically a related but distinct species) due to a Tasha-era sensitivity-read concern about the term 'Arcane' being already overloaded. Spelljammer purists prefer the original name and lore.

question: Before Ravenloft (1983), Tracy Hickman wrote a trilogy of 1982-1983 modules called the Desert of Desolation series, set in a fictional Arabian-inspired desert region of the Forgotten Realms. The three modules are I3, I4, I5. The middle module sends the PCs into a pyramid tomb of a long-dead Pharaoh, ultimately confronting his lich form. What was the lich-pharaoh's name?
answer: Amun-Re, sometimes spelled Amon-Re in different printings
choices: Amun-Re, sometimes spelled Amon-Re in different printings
Set-Anu, the Lord of the Black Lands of Athas
Khepri-Atum, the Sun Pharaoh of the lost dynasty
Imhotep-Ra, the Architect-King of the great pyramid
context: The Desert of Desolation trilogy: I3 Pharaoh (1982), I4 Oasis of the White Palm (1982), I5 Lost Tomb of Martek (1983). The series was popular enough that TSR compiled it as a single supermodule in 1987. The 'Pharaoh's Box' magic item from I3 is iconic among TSR collectors. Tracy Hickman has cited the modules as his proving-ground writing exercises before tackling Dragonlance and Ravenloft. The Egyptian-inspired Mulhorand region of the Forgotten Realms eventually absorbed the setting.

question: After WotC bought TSR in 1997, the company launched a major rules overhaul in 2000 — D&D 3rd Edition — built around a unified d20 mechanic and an Open Game License that let third-party publishers freely use the rules. The lead designers were Jonathan Tweet, Monte Cook, and Skip Williams. Which 1995-2000 D&D-adjacent game system did the 3rd Edition d20 mechanic most directly derive from?
answer: Roll-over d20 vs target number, evolved from Alternity (1998) and basic d20 mechanics in many TSR products
choices: Roll-over d20 vs target number, evolved from Alternity (1998) and basic d20 mechanics in many TSR products
Roll-under d20 vs attribute, used in the BRP-based Call of Cthulhu and RuneQuest games
Pool of d10s, similar to Vampire the Masquerade's Storyteller system
Roll 3d6, used in GURPS and Champions (Hero System) games
context: The d20 System Reference Document (SRD) launch in 2000 under the Open Game License was revolutionary — it let companies like Paizo (publishers of Dungeon Magazine post-2002) create products built on D&D's chassis. The OGL was responsible for the indie-RPG boom of the 2000s and ultimately Paizo's 2009 Pathfinder, which used a modified d20 chassis. WotC tried to revoke the OGL in 2023 — sparking a major backlash that resulted in the OGL 1.0a being permanently released to the public domain.

question: Mordenkainen's apprentice and friend in Gygax's Greyhawk campaign was a wizard whose magical hand-creating spells became iconic — Bigby's Interposing Hand, Bigby's Grasping Hand, Bigby's Forceful Hand, Bigby's Crushing Hand, Bigby's Clenched Fist. Bigby was the campaign character of one of TSR's earliest employees. Whose home-campaign character was Bigby?
answer: Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-DM and TSR co-founder
choices: Rob Kuntz, Gygax's co-DM and TSR co-founder
Tim Kask, the original editor of Dragon Magazine
Brian Blume, Gygax's TSR business partner
James Ward, of Metamorphosis Alpha fame
context: Rob Kuntz (1955-) co-DM'd the Greyhawk campaign with Gygax from 1972 onwards. His main character Robilar (a fighter) and his second character Bigby (a wizard) both became iconic Greyhawk NPCs. Robilar famously joined Mordenkainen and others in the Citadel of Eight (later the Circle of Eight). Kuntz worked at TSR from 1976 until the late 1980s as a designer. He has spent decades documenting his Greyhawk-era home-game material and writing his own systems.

question: The visual identity of classic D&D was set by a small group of staff artists at TSR in the late 1970s and early 1980s. The most distinctive style — psychedelic, weird, slightly Gothic — belonged to one artist whose creature illustrations in the 1977 Monster Manual and 1981 Moldvay Basic D&D rulebook defined the aesthetic. Who was the artist?
choices: David Trampier — DMG and Monster Manual interior art
Jeff Easley — covers of 1983-1989 AD&D hardcovers
context: Erol Otus (1956-) joined TSR in 1979 and left around 1982 for freelance work. His distinctive bold-color compositions and weirdly-proportioned monsters became visual shorthand for early-1980s D&D. Otus illustrated the Moldvay Basic D&D rulebook cover (1981) and many beloved Monster Manual interior pieces. The other major staff artists were David Trampier (DMG cover, MM interior), Jeff Dee (the Underworld and Wilderness Adventures box art), Larry Elmore (later 1980s covers, Dragonlance), Jeff Easley, and Clyde Caldwell. Each had a distinct visual style.

question: Rob Kuntz's home-campaign fighter Robilar became infamous in Greyhawk lore for breaking into Castle Greyhawk (Gygax's home-campaign mega-dungeon) and slaughtering most of its monsters and traps with mid-1970s play. In a 1975 session, Robilar and Mordenkainen together explored the deepest level of Castle Greyhawk and confronted the most powerful demon in the entire complex. What demon-lord did they face?
answer: Zuggtmoy, the Demon Queen of Fungi
choices: Zuggtmoy, the Demon Queen of Fungi
Lolth, the Demon Queen of Spiders
Demogorgon, the Prince of Demons himself
Iuz, the cambion demigod of the Flanaess
context: Zuggtmoy was first mentioned in Gygax's Greyhawk play sessions in 1973-1975 before her formal publication in the 1985 Temple of Elemental Evil. Robilar and Mordenkainen 'defeated' her in the deepest level of Castle Greyhawk — though Gygax later said the encounter ended with the demon being imprisoned rather than destroyed, setting up her later return as the central villain of T1-4. The 'Castle Greyhawk' dungeon itself was the original D&D megadungeon, and Gygax's home-campaign play notes (later somewhat published) are sought-after collector's items.

question: Chaosium's 1981 Call of Cthulhu RPG translated Lovecraft's cosmic horror into a tabletop format with the iconic 'Sanity Score' mechanic. A character's Sanity points decrease as they witness cosmic horror; reach zero and the character goes permanently insane. The system spawned over 40 years of supplements and remains one of the longest-running RPGs ever. Who designed it?
answer: Sandy Petersen, who later did level design on id Software's Doom and Quake
choices: Sandy Petersen, who later did level design on id Software's Doom and Quake
Steve Perrin, the original RuneQuest fantasy-game system designer
Greg Stafford, the legendary creator of the Glorantha setting
Ken St. Andre, the irascible Tunnels and Trolls designer
context: Sandy Petersen (1955-) is a deeply religious Mormon designer who somehow became the world's foremost interpreter of cosmic-horror gaming. After Call of Cthulhu, he designed RuneQuest III and worked on id Software's Doom (1993) and Quake (1996). The 'level designer' role he pioneered at id influenced first-person shooter design forever. He returned to tabletop in the 2010s with his own company, Petersen Games, making Lovecraftian and historical board games.

question: Chaosium's 1978 RuneQuest fantasy RPG, designed by Steve Perrin, was set in a richly-detailed Bronze Age fantasy world featuring elaborate cult-based religion, dragon-newts, dwarves who were sentient machinery, ducks who were sentient ducks, and the constant tension between Lunar and Solar empires. The setting was the original creation of one specific person — Chaosium's founder. Who created Glorantha?
answer: Greg Stafford, founder of Chaosium and Glorantha mythologist
choices: Greg Stafford, founder of Chaosium and Glorantha mythologist
Steve Perrin, the RuneQuest rules designer
Sandy Petersen, the Call of Cthulhu designer
Lynn Willis, the Chaosium editor and designer
context: Greg Stafford (1948-2018) built Glorantha as a personal worldbuilding project starting in the 1960s — like Ed Greenwood with Forgotten Realms, but with a deeper anthropological framing. Glorantha drew on Eliade's Patterns in Comparative Religion as a structural inspiration. Stafford spent his entire life refining the setting; HeroQuest, Pendragon (1985), and the more recent 13th Age in Glorantha all drew on his core lore. Stafford was inducted into the Origins Awards Hall of Fame in 2013. He died in 2018.

question: Game Designers' Workshop's 1977 sci-fi RPG Traveller, designed by Marc Miller, established many of the conventions of sci-fi roleplaying. Its character generation was famous for one specific innovation: characters served careers (Navy, Marines, Scouts, Merchants, Army, Other) for multiple four-year terms, gaining skills but risking death. If you 'died' during chargen, you actually rolled up a new character. What was this signature mechanic called?
answer: Survival rolls during chargen — characters could literally die before play began
choices: Survival rolls during chargen — characters could literally die before play began
Reincarnation tables — death meant a new body but the same character
Critical career failure — death meant career change, not actual death
Random aging effects — repeated terms reduced physical stats but not death
context: Traveller's death-during-chargen mechanic became famously controversial — some saw it as adding gritty realism, others as just frustrating. Later Traveller editions made the rule optional. The game's setting, the Third Imperium, has been a constantly-developing universe since 1977. Marc Miller still oversees the line, now published as Mongoose Traveller (2008+). Traveller is considered one of the most influential RPGs ever, alongside D&D, RuneQuest, and Call of Cthulhu.

question: Hero Games' 1981 superhero RPG Champions, designed by Steve Peterson and George MacDonald, was the first major game built around 'point-buy' character creation — players spent character-construction points to design custom powers, advantages, and disadvantages. The system became modular and was eventually used for fantasy (Fantasy Hero), espionage (Espionage), and sci-fi (Star Hero) games. What was the umbrella system name?
answer: The Hero System, also called Champions Hero System
choices: The Hero System, also called Champions Hero System
The GURPS System, the Steve Jackson Games universal mechanic
The Storyteller System, the White Wolf World of Darkness mechanic
The FATE System, an early Fudge-derivative game
context: The Hero System reached its definitive form in 4th Edition (1989), with revisions through 6th Edition (2009). The system's signature feature is the granularity of power design — every superpower or magical effect could be deconstructed into 'mechanics' bought separately. Champions itself remains in print as the flagship Hero System game. Hero Games' tabletop RPG The Champions of New Olympus has appeared in superhero-RPG canon since 1981 alongside Mayfair Games' DC Heroes and TSR's Marvel Super Heroes.

question: West End Games' 1984 dystopian-comedy RPG Paranoia, designed by Greg Costikyan, Dan Gelber, and Eric Goldberg, satirized Cold War paranoia by setting the game in a future totalitarian complex run by an insane AI 'Computer.' Players are Troubleshooters whose job is to find and report traitors — while being themselves traitors. Every player character has 'clearance' (Red, Orange, Yellow, Green, Blue, Indigo, Violet, Ultra-Violet). What was the brand of the player handbook's notorious cover slogan?
answer: 'Stay Alert! Trust No One! Keep Your Laser Handy!'
choices: 'Stay Alert! Trust No One! Keep Your Laser Handy!'
'You Are Safe! The Computer Is Your Friend! Report Everything!'
'Welcome To Alpha Complex! Have A Nice Day! Don't Die!'
'Service The Computer! Report All Mutants! Watch Out For Communists!'
context: Paranoia's tone was deliberately satirical — Costikyan was a libertarian-leaning author whose intent was a comedic critique of authoritarianism (the Computer thinks it's helping; the players are forced to lie and betray to survive). The game spawned multiple editions through Mongoose Publishing (2004 onwards). Greg Costikyan went on to write extensively about game design theory. The phrase 'The Computer is your friend' became a tongue-in-cheek meme outside the gaming hobby.

question: Gygax's 1978 S1 Tomb of Horrors module contains a famously specific trap involving the demilich Acererak's final form. After the PCs defeat his minions and pass through the tomb's puzzles, they reach Acererak's burial chamber. His skull rests on a pile of gems. When approached, the demilich rises and attacks. The skull has six gems set in its eye sockets, with very specific effects. What happens when a player tries to take one of the gems?
answer: Each gem holds the trapped soul of an adventurer Acererak previously defeated; touching releases the demilich's life-draining attack
choices: Each gem holds the trapped soul of an adventurer Acererak previously defeated; touching releases the demilich's life-draining attack
Each gem is a sphere of annihilation in disguise; touching disintegrates the PC instantly
Each gem is a wish-spell trapped in physical form; touching grants the wish but kills the PC
Each gem is an alternate timeline of the PC; touching merges the PC with the alternate, causing alignment loss
context: Acererak's gems include diamond, ruby, jet, fire opal, large opal, and emerald. Each represents a different soul-trapping mechanism — touching one drains levels, another forces a saving throw vs death, another permanently traps the PC's soul. The demilich form is a skull animated by the lich's residual willpower; it can only be defeated by destroying the gems AND the skull. Some 1e modules and later 5e adaptations have player characters who unsealed an Acererak gem decades earlier returning to the game as freed (but missing-souled) characters.

question: Fritz Leiber's Fafhrd and the Gray Mouser stories appeared in Weird Tales and other pulp magazines starting in 1939, but the two characters were originally created by Leiber and his college friend Harry Otto Fischer in 1934. The original first Fafhrd-Mouser story was titled with what specific phrase, later anthologized in the collection 'Swords and Deviltry' (1970)?
answer: 'Two Sought Adventure' — the original 1939 Weird Tales publication title
choices: 'Two Sought Adventure' — the original 1939 Weird Tales publication title
'The Jewels in the Forest' — the second-published Fafhrd-Mouser story
'Ill Met in Lankhmar' — the Hugo-winning 1970 novella
context: 'Two Sought Adventure' (1939) was retitled 'The Jewels in the Forest' for later collections. Leiber wrote Fafhrd-Mouser stories continuously from 1939 until his death in 1992, eventually filling seven collected volumes. 'Ill Met in Lankhmar' (1970) won the Hugo and Nebula awards for Best Novella — the only Fafhrd-Mouser story to win major awards. The collection 'Swords and Deviltry' compiled the earliest stories chronologically. Lankhmar itself, the city of Black Toga, is the most-developed city in classic sword-and-sorcery.

question: Gary Gygax's original home-campaign mega-dungeon, Castle Greyhawk, was the playtesting ground for D&D from 1972 onwards. The dungeon had multiple levels — Gygax himself ran it for years with his home group. The exact level count varies in different sources. According to Gygax's own 1979 Dragon Magazine retrospective and his later Castle Zagyg series, how many levels did Castle Greyhawk have in its mature form?
answer: Thirteen named levels, with sub-levels and dimensional pockets adding many more sections
choices: Thirteen named levels, with sub-levels and dimensional pockets adding many more sections
Ten levels of identical 20-by-20 hex rooms, with no significant deeper sections
Twenty-five themed levels, including elemental zones and a Far Realm gateway
Seven levels matching the classical seven-planet medieval astrology
context: Castle Greyhawk's design was idiosyncratic, with thematic levels (the Magic-User Level, the Trap Level, the Demonic Level), multiple stairways between levels, and dimensional pockets. The infamous 'Tomb of Tsojcanth' was one such pocket. Gygax began publishing partial Castle Greyhawk material via his post-TSR company Troll Lord Games in 2005 — Castle Zagyg (Yggsburgh + The East Mark of the Flanaess) before his 2008 death. The full mega-dungeon material was eventually published in 2008-2011 by Troll Lord, but the Gygax estate has restricted later printings.

question: R.A. Salvatore introduced Drizzt Do'Urden as a last-minute addition to The Crystal Shard (1988) — his editor Mary Kirchoff had asked for a 'sidekick' for the human ranger protagonist. Salvatore offered a renegade drow as a placeholder, expecting Kirchoff to reject the idea. The novel hadn't been pitched with Drizzt at the front, but he stole the entire trilogy and went on to anchor over thirty more Salvatore novels. Salvatore later wrote a separate prequel trilogy giving Drizzt's full origin in Menzoberranzan. What's that prequel trilogy called?
answer: The Dark Elf Trilogy: Homeland (1990), Exile (1990), Sojourn (1991)
choices: The Dark Elf Trilogy: Homeland (1990), Exile (1990), Sojourn (1991)
The Legacy Trilogy: Legacy, Starless Night, Siege of Darkness (1992-1994)
The Cleric Quintet: Canticle, In Sylvan Shadows, Night Masks, Fallen Fortress, Chaos Curse (1991-1994)
The Hunter's Blades Trilogy: Thousand Orcs, Lone Drow, Two Swords (2002-2004)
context: The Dark Elf Trilogy is widely considered Salvatore's best work and the definitive depiction of drow society. Homeland (1990) showed Drizzt's youth in House Do'Urden in Menzoberranzan; Exile (1990) showed his banishment into the Underdark wilderness; Sojourn (1991) showed his journey to the surface and the early friendship with the blind ranger Montolio DeBrouchee. Salvatore's portrayal of Menzoberranzan as a matriarchal drow city-state — with its noble houses, the Academy, and the constant intrigue against Lolth — became iconic Forgotten Realms canon.

question: Jack Chick's 1984 evangelical tract 'Dark Dungeons,' the most-distributed anti-D&D pamphlet of the Satanic Panic era, depicts a fictional teenage girl named Debbie being recruited into a D&D group by a 'Dungeon Master' named Ms. Frost. The group plays a session where Debbie's character earns levels of magic. Frost then invites Debbie to a real witchcraft circle, where she learns 'real spells.' One specific spell Debbie casts on her father is named in the tract. What does she cast on him?
answer: A 'Mind Bondage' spell that puts him in a hypnotic state
choices: A 'Mind Bondage' spell that puts him in a hypnotic state
A 'Charm Person' spell directly copied from D&D
A 'Cause Disease' spell that makes him fall ill
A 'Curse of Failure' spell that destroys his business
context: The Mind Bondage spell in the tract was Jack Chick's invention, not drawn from any actual D&D spell-list. The tract ends with Debbie's friend Marcie killing herself after her D&D character 'died' (echoing the Patricia Pulling narrative), Debbie repenting and accepting Christ, and the tract burning her D&D books. The 2014 indie film 'Dark Dungeons' (directed by JR Ralls, written by Tim Skubick) adapted the tract as a deadpan straight-faced comedy with the original pamphlet's dialogue preserved verbatim. Jack Chick (1924-2016) produced hundreds of tracts on various 'evils' from rock music to Catholicism.

question: The 1982 CBS made-for-TV movie Mazes and Monsters, starring Tom Hanks as a college student named Robbie Wheeling who loses touch with reality while playing the fictional 'Mazes and Monsters' game, was Hanks' first leading role. The film's climax sends Robbie's character 'Pardieu the Holy Man' to perform a magical leap from a great height as part of his fantasy ritual. From what New York City landmark does Robbie plan to leap, believing himself to be Pardieu?
answer: The top of the World Trade Center, before being talked down
choices: The top of the World Trade Center, before being talked down
The Statue of Liberty's torch, in a foggy night sequence
The Brooklyn Bridge, during a sunrise confrontation
The Empire State Building observation deck, during midnight
context: Pardieu the Holy Man's fictional last 'task' in the game is to leap from a tall tower to reach the Two Towers of Belderak. Robbie's fantasy delusion sends him to the World Trade Center's observation deck. His friends find him at the brink. The scene's emotional climax is intercut with the parents and friends realizing what's been happening to him. Tom Hanks said in a 2018 interview that he was 'mortified' to learn the film was now considered a Satanic Panic artifact, when at the time he just thought it was a serious-issues TV movie. Mazes and Monsters has become an ironic cult favorite at retro tabletop conventions.
